drafts.title: Hyundai Ioniq 5 still prints a real Sep payment. Shop the stack, not the sticker.
drafts.window: 11 AM-2 PM MT Thursday (secondary Thu ~10 AM).
drafts.angle: Outside California, Sep Ioniq 5 SE Standard Range leases from about $319/mo for 24 months with $4,999 due; SE RWD long-range about $329. Also 0% APR up to 60-72 months and up to ~$5,000 savings outside CA. Kitchen-table: payment + insurance + home charge before you sign.
bullets: Electrek (Sep 15, 2026): 2026 Ioniq 5 starts ~$35,000; first-half 2026 best-selling non-Tesla EV in the US.
Outside CA: leases from ~$319/mo (24 mo, $4,999 due) on SE Standard Range (~245 mi); SE RWD long-range ~$329/mo (~318 mi).
CA leases from ~$329/mo (24 mo, $4,999 due); possible extra MyFirstEV discount in CA.
Finance path: 0% APR up to 60 months (Electrek also notes up to 72 months on some offers) + 0 payments for 90 days, or up to ~$3,000-$5,000 discount paths depending on region.
Soft-pedal Bolt LIVE and Wed Niro leftover; this is the Ioniq payment stack.
drafts.body:
Hyundai just kept the Ioniq 5 in the "real family math" lane for September.

Outside California, the SE Standard Range lease starts around $319 a month for 24 months with about $4,999 due at signing. Bump to the longer-range SE RWD and you are nearer $329 a month for roughly 318 miles of EPA range. There is also a 0% APR path with a few months of payment holiday on some offers, plus regional cash discounts.

That is not a mandate story. That is a payment story.

US kitchen-table take for a 42-year-old commuting in Colorado, or a 58-year-old replacing a paid-off crossover:

1) Get the out-the-door payment in writing for the exact trim and destination fee.
2) Quote insurance on that VIN before you sign (see Framework 4).
3) Map weekday charging: Level 2 at home, workplace, or a real apartment plan if you rent.
4) Road-trip once on a public charger so the app and the rate are not a surprise.

35-54 line: the Ioniq 5 is still one of the few non-Tesla EVs with a national lease you can actually budget. Your win is the monthly stack, not the brochure.

55+ line: 0% and a clear lease only help if insurance and the plug plan keep your independence.

drafts.title: Kia EV3 Wind at about $349 a month. The affordable ladder just got a new rung.
drafts.angle: 2027 Kia EV3 Light starts ~$29,890 (221 mi). Wind FWD starts ~$34,990 (up to 321 mi) with advertised lease ~$349/mo for 24 months and $3,999 due. Soft-pedal Bolt LIVE. Kitchen-table: compare effective monthly cost, not headline monthlies.
bullets: Electrek (Sep 10, 2026): EV3 Light FWD ~$29,890 / ~221 mi; Wind FWD ~$34,990 / up to 321 mi; AWD adds ~$3,200.
Advertised Wind FWD lease ~$349/mo with $3,999 due (24 mo in Electrek article; Electrek lease guide also lists Wind RWD ~$349/36 mo factory line).
Wind AWD special lease ~$399/mo with $3,999 due (24 mo per Electrek).
Also 0.90% APR financing up to 48 months; Light trim may lack a national lease.
Standard NACS port on EV3 trims (Tesla Supercharger access without a separate adapter).
drafts.body:
Kia put a new rung on the affordable EV ladder.

The 2027 EV3 Light starts near $29,890 with about 221 miles of range. The Wind FWD starts nearer $34,990 and can reach about 321 miles. Kia is advertising Wind leases around $349 a month with about $3,999 due at signing. There is also a cheap APR finance path on some trims.

Headline monthlies lie if you ignore drive-off cash. Add the due-at-signing, divide by the months, then add insurance and your real charge plan.

US kitchen-table take:

1) Ask for the effective monthly (payment + drive-off amortized), not just the ad number.
2) Confirm which battery and drive (Light vs Wind, FWD vs AWD) is on the contract.
3) Quote insurance on that VIN.
4) If you rent, map a plug before you fall in love with the range sticker.

35-54 line: a 321-mile Wind at a mid-$300s lease is the kind of number Premium timelines actually save.

55+ line: start with the Light sticker only if the Wind payment still fits your fixed income after insurance.

drafts.body:
If you need three rows and a normal dealer experience, the Prologue is still in the conversation.

Electrek's September manufacturer table still shows a Honda Prologue AWD Touring near $279 a month for 36 months with about $5,099 due at signing. That works out nearer $413 a month once you average the drive-off. Some dealers advertise even lower monthlies. Always verify the exact sheet for your ZIP.

This is not a robotaxi thread. This is "can we replace the aging gas SUV without lighting the budget on fire."

US kitchen-table checklist:

1) Get the Prologue quote and an Ioniq 5 or Mach-E quote the same afternoon.
2) Same insurance shop for each VIN.
3) Same home or apartment charge plan.
4) Pick the one that wins on total monthly pain, not the prettiest screen.

35-54 line: family SUV money that Premium accounts actually bookmark.

55+ line: a normal service lane and a written payment beat a futuristic demo every time.

drafts.title: EVs still cost more to insure on average. Quote the VIN before you fall in love.
drafts.angle: Insurify 2026: full-coverage EV average ~$3,159/yr vs gas ~$2,218 (~42% higher). Newer models (2024+) gap shrinks to ~18% (~$501/yr). Colorado newer-EV gap ~22% in their state table. Soft-pedal Tesla order-page insurance LIVE; this is national EV-vs-gas math + shop-before-sign.
bullets: Insurify EV insurance report: average full-coverage EV ~$3,159/yr vs gas ~$2,218/yr across model years (~42% / ~$941 gap).
Newer models (2024+): gap ~18% / ~$501 per year.
Colorado row (newer): EV ~$3,977 vs gas ~$3,249 (~22%).
Newer EV insurance rates fell ~11.1% over the last year vs ~7.7% for newer gas (Insurify).
Tip from same report: shop insurance before you pick the car; deductible and multi-policy discounts matter.
drafts.body:
The payment can look fine and the insurance can still wreck the deal.

Insurify's 2026 numbers put average full-coverage EV insurance near $3,159 a year. Gas cars in the same dataset average nearer $2,218. That is roughly a 42 percent gap across all model years. On newer cars the gap shrinks toward 18 percent, about $500 a year. In Colorado their newer-EV row sits roughly 22 percent above newer gas.

That is not a reason to panic. It is a reason to get a real quote on the exact VIN before you sign.

US kitchen-table move:

1) Pick two trims you actually like.
2) Send both VINs (or year/make/model/ZIP) to two insurers the same morning.
3) Add the better quote to the lease or finance payment.
4) Only then decide if the EV still wins on total monthly cost after fuel savings.

35-54 line: Premium timelines love a concrete dollar gap. Give them the VIN step.

55+ line: do not let a surprise premium eat the independence you bought the EV for.

drafts.title: Soft costs still hide in solar quotes. Ask if your city runs SolarAPP+.
drafts.angle: Soft costs (permit, inspection, interconnection, delays) often rival hardware. SolarAPP+ (DOE/NREL) can issue eligible residential solar permits instantly in adopting AHJs. Soft-pedal CA AB 1738 LIVE (remote inspection $600-$1,000). This is national "ask your installer" soft-cost literacy, not a CA bill rehash.
bullets: NREL/industry soft-cost framing: permitting + inspection + interconnection are a real line item; delay/rework can dominate the true cost.
SolarAPP+ (gosolarapp.org): automated code-compliance review; eligible residential solar / solar+storage permits can issue instantly in participating jurisdictions.
Adoption list maintained publicly; updated into 2026 (check your city/county on the map).
Homeowner move: demand an itemized permit/interconnection line and ask whether SolarAPP+ or another expedited path is live locally.
Soft-pedal AB 1738 LIVE and battery-heavy rebate maps.
drafts.body:
Solar panels get the Instagram shot. Soft costs get your wallet.

Permits, inspections, interconnection paperwork, and rework can quietly add thousands depending on your zip code. Some cities still move on paper timelines. Others plug into SolarAPP+, a DOE/NREL tool that can approve eligible residential solar jobs in minutes instead of weeks.

You do not need to become a permit geek. You need one question on the quote.

US kitchen-table script for a 48-year-old homeowner (or a 65-year-old on a fixed roof budget):

1) "Show me permit, inspection, and interconnection as separate lines."
2) "Does our AHJ use SolarAPP+ or another same-day path?"
3) "Who pays if the first inspection fails?"
4) "What is the bill savings math on MY rate, not a national average?"

35-54 line: soft costs are where families get surprised after the shiny panel pitch.

55+ line: itemized paperwork is how you keep independence without a change-order spiral.
